Cape Town keeping the lights on for longer

By: Liz Fish | Paid

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
This weekend the rest of the country had Stage 1 load shedding but there was none in Cape Town and rugby fans were able to watch the final of the Wales vs SA and the stadium was bursting with fans. The secret is the Steenbras dam, it acts as a massive battery that is charged up to be used when the power is down providing 180MW more power into the Cities grid. It keeps Cape Town between 1 and two stages less load shedding.

Summary:
But apart from Cape Town’s secret weapon which they keep very well maintained and plan to expand, currently limited by the storage capacity of the lower reservoir there are many other power projects afoot to unshackle their dependency on Eskom.
Cape Town’s Mayor Geordin Hill Lewis is making major strides in breaking the shackles that national Government have placed on Municipalities. He says the legislation is so confusing about whether municipalities can procure their own power Cape Town is just going ahead. At the end of June was the closing date for IPP submissions, 200 MW of renewal power will be commission and by the beginning of next year they will commission the projects bringing in new power by 2025. The bigger picture is that the more secure the power supply in the Western Cape the more they can attract business.


Further information:
The City is essentially liberalizing the access to power and actively encouraging residents and businesses to procure power. They are piloting something called Wheeling. A power producer for example in the Northern Cape can sell power directly to a business in Cape Town using the Eskom or City grid. The producer must generate 1MW of power or more and the pilot is to work out the tariffs and how distribution network will function. There is already provision within NERSA regulations for wheeling but this is doing it on a larger scale.

Geordian Hill Lewis says it will be a neural charge to use the grid but more importantly “Because the price paid for energy by the parties to a power purchase agreement relying on wheeling is not fixed by the state, the implementation of this policy is also an important first step towards energy market liberalization in South Africa.”
On a smaller scale but not insignificant generating between 50/60 MW of power is SSEG Small Scale Embedded Generation.

Currently there are 2335 customers currently but rapidly expanding as more people turn to solar power. Residents and business feed their excess power into the grid and their municipal bills are credited. In the past they had to be a net user by Hill Lewis has lifted the restrictions on business enabling them to produce a much solar as they can and get cash back for their investment. The City installs a bi-directional metering and monitoring system using a NERSA approved feed-in tariff. They get paid a R1 off the R2.50 unit price.

Script:


Opening sequence to music
Link “I have a lot of social media apps on my phone, but lately I feel like I am check my the loadshedding app- more than any of them, constantly checking the schedule
Script: It’s been a pretty grim few weeks - never knowing when the lights would be on…and when Eskom warned stage 8 was expected - you can imagine what a nightmare it was for Cape Town mayor - Geordin Hill Lewis.
Geordin “ Stage eight is a real nightmare scenario. All of our city services, things like water stations, water purification stations, sewage pump stations, all of our electricity substations would run out of battery, they wouldn't have enough time to recharge. Your cell phone towers would run out of battery- There's very little that we could have done about it to save residents in Cape Town from a real, real catastrophe.

Script: But this week - the whole picture changed with President Cyril Ramaphosa’s family meeting.

Ramaphosa “ The crisis that we are facing requires that we should take bold, courageous and decisive action to close the electricity gap in our country.

Script: In one fell swoop, he ended Eskom's monopoly on power production…lifting the limits on those Municipalities that can afford to buy power from Independent producers. For energy specialist Vincenizo Belleni, it’s been a very good week.

Vinnie: It's a huge game changer. What it's doing, it's enabling the industry to do what the industry wants to do, and that is supply energy. But as importantly, it's also enabling businesses to flourish and the economy to flourish and allows the economy and the businesses to choose where they want to buy the power from, and how much they want to pay.

Script: I was shocked to discover that throughout this whole crisis, Cape Town has had less load shedding than the rest of the country. It’s something many Capetonians may not even know. It's all because of this high mountain, and a 40-year-old hydro pump station at Steenbras Dam, which has been kept in excellent condition.

Link: This is the ace up Cape Town’s sleeve, basically put this hydropump station is the reason Cape Town is experiencing load shedding to a lesser degree than the rest of the country
Script: It’s a simple process - water is released from the top dam- driving 4 turbines, to generate power for Cape Town in morning and evening peak periods. At night, it's pumped back to the top…ready for the next day.
Geordin: Every stage of load shedding costs Cape Town 75 million rand per stage, per day

Masa 75 million rand Per stage per day.

Geordin “ So we can protect Cape Town from two stages, which means we can save the Cape Town economy from 150 million rand in losses every day

Script: Since becoming mayor, he’s been on a mission for the City to take matters into its own hands, and break its dependence on Eskom. In June, they began the process of commissioning power, from independent producers.

Geordin: Our singular obsession is making up that load shedding gap and that is about 4 to 500 megawatts

LINK: The City of Cape Town played a pivotal role in a drawn-out legal battle which finally allowed municipalities to buy and generate their own power. Now the president has lifted the remaining restrictions and promised to simplify the legislation.
Masa: does this mean that the legislation will also change and ease up and it won't be as bogged down as it was before?

Vinnie: So there's already been an announcement by the Department of Environmental Affairs that they are going to cut down on the environmental processing times. And now with the president bringing all the departments together to form this one stop shop,it's going to take their preparation from three years, possibly down to about six months.

Geordin: I hope it sends a very clear message to Nersa in particular, that the registration process should be a matter of days, not weeks, not months, and certainly not years. It sends a message to the Minister of Energy, that he should not stand in municipalities and cities way who are trying to do this, there's no need for ministerial permission we can get on with it.

Link: We are all fed up with high electricity prices and load shedding - and anyone who can afford to install a solar systems is doing so – some are selling their excess power back to the city
Script: It’s known as small scale embedded generation - SSEG . Businessman Micheal MacLachlan sells excess power back to the City from his home, and shopping centre.
Michael: This complex generates about 40% of what it consumes. And we also do push back into the grid a small amount when in non-peak times, which means that we get about a 43% savings off our electricity bill.
Masa: Could you tell us how the tariffs work?

Michael: I mean, obviously, tariffs differ between different residential and commercial. Our tariff here is currently approximately two rand per kilowatt hour that we consume when we feed back into the grid and they pay us back approximately one rand per kilowatt that we feed back into the grid.

Script: In the past businesses had to consume more electricity than they sold, this week the mayor announced that the City was lifting those restrictions

Hill Lewis - There's no limits on the amount of power that you can produce in Cape Town. We will take as much as you can give us we will eft it to you we will ewallet if you want we'll send you cash for the power you send us.

Script: The president now even made it possible for Eskom to buy small-scale solar generated power from independents…overnight it’s made private solar generation a viable commercial option.
Link” While we wait for renewable energy power plants to come online, these rooftop systems represent immediately accessible power for the City of Cape Town- and there are a growing number of them across town.
Script: Tony Sutter is the head of Facilities Management at the mammoth Old Mutual Park in Pinelands. Their electricity bill was R48 Million a year before they installed solar…and to date- it’s saved them R17 million. For the moment, they don’t have excess power to sell
Masa: The recent announcements by the Cape Town mayor and the president, how does that change things for you long term?

Tony: So that gives us another opportunity, to produce significantly more on our, on our carbon reduction strategy. The announcement really strengthens that business case, not just from a carbon business, but it gives us a strong commercial business case, where we can then sell overproduced energy back on back to the grid.

Script: But after the mayor’s announcement, - they decided to put a whole solar field on land nearby
PAUSE
Cape Town is piloting something known as Wheeling - it’s where a business can buy electricity directly from a power producer, using the City, or Eskom’s grid. What still needs to be thrashed out are the tariffs to use the grid
Vinnie: most people think Cape Town's a tourist destination. If it had more wheeled energy, it would be more attractive for international investors. It would be more attractive for factories to set up shop here. The economy would really flourish with more energy being available, which can only be achieved through wheeling

Masa: What would you say the city's energy mix would look like in the next five years?

Geordin: We're going to take from a lot of different strands. We're going to take a little bit from SSEG We're going to take quite a lot from independent power producers. We're going to get some storage. All together, that mix is going to add up to us being about 20% self-reliant. And that is enough to end load shedding. Remember, that is our goal.

Script: It’s been an exciting week – and the Mother City is ready to share its plans.
Masa: It sounds like we can finally smile, there is light at the end of the tunnel.

Vinnie: There's light at the end of the tunnel. It's not an oncoming train. And the president made a fundamental shift to liberalizing the market.
